title: Coding Turing computations

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 38–41 (§2.6, numerical configurations and finite computation histories; version 2007-01-09)

summary: Encode finite tape contents, construct primitive-recursive numerical transitions, and prove that every Turing-computed partial function is partial recursive.
abstract: When a tape head moves right, the symbol it just wrote becomes the nearest cell on its left. Recording the current symbol and two finite lists therefore turns a tape computation into changes to finite data. Pairing and list codes turn those changes into numerical operations, including a precise rule for moving into an unrecorded blank cell. For each fixed Turing machine, initialization, one transition, the halt test and the final readout can all be constructed by primitive recursion. The numerical run preserves an explicit relation to the machine's actual tape, so it has exactly the same halting inputs and outputs. A finite successful run can then be checked by a primitive-recursive test, and searching for such a record proves that every Turing-computed partial function is partial recursive. The argument allows arbitrary finite alphabets and state sets; extra recorded blanks need not give a unique code.
